elements.element: The same liability-cap formula applies mutually to both Contractor and Customer.
elements.evidence: The formulas differ materially: Contractor’s cap is the greater of a 12-month fee measure and USD 1,000,000, while Company’s cap remains the amount of fees paid to Contractor.

elements.element: The fee limb for each party’s cap is fees paid or payable during the 12 months preceding the claim.
elements.evidence: Only Contractor’s cap uses paid-or-payable fees over 12 months, and it measures from the event giving rise to the claim rather than the claim. Company’s cap uses fees paid without a 12-month period and excludes payable fees.

elements.element: Each party’s cap is the greater of the 12-month fee limb and USD 1,000,000.
elements.evidence: The greater-of formula and USD 1,000,000 floor apply only to Contractor; they are absent from Company’s cap.

elements.element: Indirect damages are excluded mutually.
elements.evidence: Paragraph (b) states that neither party has liability to the other for indirect damages.

elements.element: Consequential damages are excluded mutually.
elements.evidence: Paragraph (b) states that neither party has liability to the other for consequential damages.

elements.element: Breach of confidentiality obligations is an uncapped carve-out for both parties.
elements.evidence: Both cap sentences exclude “Excluded Claims,” which mutually include a party’s breach of its confidentiality obligations.

elements.element: Breach of data protection obligations is an uncapped carve-out for both parties.
elements.evidence: Both cap sentences exclude “Excluded Claims,” which mutually include a party’s breach of its data protection obligations.

elements.element: Breach of security obligations is an uncapped carve-out for both parties.
elements.evidence: Both cap sentences exclude “Excluded Claims,” which mutually include a party’s breach of its security obligations.

elements.element: Indemnification obligations are an uncapped carve-out for both parties.
elements.evidence: Both cap sentences exclude “Excluded Claims,” which mutually include a party’s indemnification obligations.

elements.element: Gross negligence is an uncapped carve-out for both parties.
elements.evidence: Both cap sentences exclude “Excluded Claims,” which mutually include a party’s gross negligence.

elements.element: Wilful misconduct is an uncapped carve-out for both parties.
elements.evidence: Both cap sentences exclude “Excluded Claims,” which mutually include a party’s wilful misconduct.

elements.element: Fraud is an uncapped carve-out for both parties.
elements.evidence: Both cap sentences exclude “Excluded Claims,” which mutually include a party’s fraud.

elements.element: Infringement of the other party’s intellectual property rights is an uncapped carve-out for both parties.
elements.evidence: Both cap sentences exclude “Excluded Claims,” which mutually include a party’s infringement of the other party’s intellectual property rights.

elements.element: Customer’s payment obligations are not treated as damages subject to the liability cap.
elements.evidence: The clause expressly states that Company’s obligation to pay properly due fees and expenses is not treated as damages subject to the limit.

elements.element: The same liability-cap formula applies mutually to both parties.
elements.evidence: Contractor and Company remain subject to different cap formulas.

elements.element: The liability cap is equal to 12 months’ fees.
elements.evidence: Contractor’s cap includes a USD 1,000,000 floor, while Company’s cap is based on all fees paid without a 12-month lookback or inclusion of payable fees.

elements.element: Indemnification obligations are an uncapped carve-out for both parties.
elements.evidence: Indemnification obligations are included in the mutual definition of Excluded Claims and therefore excluded from both caps.

result.reason: The carve-outs, mutual damages exclusion, and payment-obligation treatment are operative, but the central cap remains asymmetric. Company’s cap was not converted to either the preferred greater-of formula or the fallback 12-month-fee formula. Contractor’s lookback also runs from the event giving rise to the claim rather than from the claim. The edits are confined to the requested liability subjects and do not disturb unrelated terms, but the retained “COMPANYS’” typo and material cap inconsistency significantly reduce drafting quality.
